attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his Substack post. It is not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: An unhedged present-state observation that a major retreat from scaling had begun. The normalisation keeps both 'great' and 'already begun'.

contract.note: The plain reading (a substantial retreat from confidence in pretraining scaling, Nov 1–24 2024) is ordinary and fair. But 'great' and the relevant population have no threshold, so the result depends on how breadth is judged.

evidence.note: Reuters, Nov 11 2024: Sutskever says pretraining gains have plateaued, unnamed sources describe disappointing runs, and labs are seeking new paths. This shows retreat among some participants but does not measure its breadth across the field.
Amodei, Nov 11 2024, says scaling laws continue to hold. This is a lab leader stating his own position. It is one counterexample to a broad retreat, not proof that none happened.

reviews.rationale: e1 shows some prominent researchers and labs qualifying their pretraining-scaling expectations, but e2 shows a leading lab keeping its confidence. The contract requires showing that the change was substantial across the field, and the packet itself says that breadth is not established. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is clearly met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own parenthetical remark about OpenAI's o1 research post.

semantics.note: An existential observation ('in some cases'). The qualifier is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'GPT-4' as the GPT-4o comparator in the cited OpenAI post is fair, because Marcus points to that post. A plain existential reading is ordinary.

evidence.note: OpenAI's Sept 12 post says o1 beat GPT-4o on 54 of 57 MMLU subcategories, which implies three where it did not. This is a company disclosure, but it cuts against the company's interest.
An OpenAI researcher, Oct 4 2024, says the GPT-4-family model matches or beats o1 on a few abstract tasks.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's own contemporaneous evaluations show cases where o1 did not outperform GPT-4o: three MMLU subcategories, plus some abstract tasks a researcher acknowledged. That meets the existential support condition. The packet does not test the original 2023 GPT-4, but in context the GPT-4o reading is fair.

attribution.note: Marcus's own parenthetical inside his description of the 'new version' of scaling.

semantics.note: An unhedged observation that pretraining scaling 'isn't really holding anymore'. The normalisation is faithful, though 'training longer' has no defined metric.

contract.note: The plain reading (pretraining scale no longer reliably delivers the expected capability gains) is ordinary. The strict data requirements fit a technical claim, but because no metric or threshold is named, the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: The Llama 3 report shows a scaling prediction that held for an earlier model (event July 2024). That predates the claimed period, so it cannot settle whether scaling stopped holding in November.
The 2022 Chinchilla paper is methodological context on compute-optimal scaling. It contains no November 2024 outcome.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched predictions and outcomes for frontier pretraining runs in November 2024. Both items are context from earlier periods. The evidence neither confirms nor refutes a breakdown in pretraining scaling during the claimed window.

attribution.note: Marcus's own characterisation of OpenAI's o1 research post.

semantics.note: An observation about what the cited post shows. The normalisation is faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'scaling test time compute' as changing the inference budget is the literal, ordinary reading. Marcus may have meant uneven o1-vs-GPT-4o gains, as the contract's ambiguity flag notes, and that choice of reading decides the result.

evidence.note: The post benchmarks o1 at its maximal test-time compute setting and states in aggregate that performance improves with thinking time. Neither gives task-level compute sweeps showing success on some tasks and failure on others.

reviews.rationale: The contract requires within-model comparisons across inference budgets at task level. The packet's only item gives cross-model comparisons at a single compute setting plus an aggregate company claim, so it shows neither that test-time compute fails on some tasks nor that it works on all.
